bibliography.checked_against: the cover and title page (PDF pp. 2 and 4: 'Technical Bulletin No. 86', Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, Madison, 1975)

claims.claim: for northern pike, egg densities in a Wisconsin lake were greatest in dense mats of sedge and wild-celery remains
claims.location: PDF p. 3, Abstract; p. 12 (PDF p. 15), Spawning conditions; p. 17 (PDF p. 20), Conclusions
claims.quote: Egg densities were greatest where dense sedge mats and wild celery remains were present
claims.conditions: Gilbert Lake, Washington County, Wisconsin (16.2 ha, mostly < 0.6 m deep, Nuphar-covered; a refuge), spawning season 1968; eggs collected with fine-mesh dip nets swept through the vegetation, 2 April–4 June 1968; densities described qualitatively (no counts are reported)
claims.note: Egg survival was poor that year: by 9–10 April very few eggs were found and few fry were caught (p. 13).

claims.claim: fewer pike eggs among bulrush stems and lily debris
claims.quote: Bottom vegetation in these other areas consisted of bulrush stems, fragments of lily pads
claims.conditions: areas of 'similar water depth and temperature but where a similar mat of vegetation was not present', where egg densities were lower; the list continues 'broken rushes, and small pieces of debris'

claims.claim: most pike eggs in dead sedge and short plant mats
claims.location: p. 17 (PDF p. 20), Conclusions; p. 12 (PDF p. 15), Environmental influences
claims.quote: wild celery, grasses, and sedges that break down to form a dense mat
claims.conditions: Gilbert Lake 1968 (the mat of last year's sedge and wild celery); 'short' is not the authors' own observation: they cite Fabricius & Gustafson (1958), who 'showed that adults deposited eggs only over dense but relatively short vegetation such as Carex spp.' (p. 12)
claims.note: The 'short' attribute should be credited 'Fabricius & Gustafson 1958, via Priegel & Krohn 1975'. The report also cites Lake George (Franklin & Smith 1963): highest egg densities in dense mats of sterile clumps of Eleocharis, next in Carex shore vegetation.

notes: Other values: spawning 25 March to the first week of April 1968, peak on the afternoons of 28–29 March at 10–17.8 °C surface water; immigration began mid-March with ice breakup and peaked at 3.4–10.6 °C (pp. 12, 17); incubation 13–16 days at 2.2–16.6 °C (p. 13); fecundity log F = −7.227 + 3.161 log L (L total length, cm; 11 females 34.0–85.6 cm), about 10,300 eggs per pound (p. 12); spawning population 2,500–3,000 in Gilbert and Big Cedar lakes; sex ratio 1 female : 2.0–2.3 males. The report recommends protecting marshes whose wild celery, grasses and sedges break down into a dense mat (p. 17).
